issue.issue_text: The legal validity and binding nature of a judicial order that interferes with the administrative authority of the Chief Justice of India regarding the constitution of benches.

facts: In response to a judicial order passed by another bench, the Chief Justice of India (CJI) found it appropriate to constitute a Constitution Bench to address the legal issues raised by that order.
law: The Chief Justice of India is the 'master of the roster,' a principle that applies to the Supreme Court just as it does to High Courts.
The CJI alone has the prerogative to constitute the Benches of the Court and allocate cases to them.
This authority is governed by precedents (like the Prakash Chand case), rules, and conventions, which are essential for judicial discipline, decorum, and the smooth functioning of the justice system.
If a bench believes a matter should be heard by a larger bench, it must refer the matter to the Chief Justice, who will then constitute such a bench.
No judge can take up a matter on their own unless it is allocated by the CJI.
application: The Court applied the 'master of the roster' principle to hold that no other bench, regardless of its size (two-judge or three-judge), can allocate a matter to itself or issue directions regarding the composition of a bench.
An order directing the CJI as to who should sit on a bench or which bench should take up a matter is an impermissible interference with the CJI's administrative authority.
The Court reasoned that allowing such orders would lead to chaos in the administration of justice and would run counter to established law and judicial discipline.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the validity of such a judicial order, declaring that any order that is contrary to the 'master of the roster' principle is to be treated as ineffective in law and is not binding on the Chief Justice of India.

arguments.issue_text: The legal validity and binding nature of a judicial order that interferes with the administrative authority of the Chief Justice of India regarding the constitution of benches.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument is not explicitly stated in the text but is implicit in the action of the two-judge bench that is being reviewed. The argument is that a judicial bench has the authority to pass an order directing that a specific matter be listed before a particular type of bench (in this case, a Constitution Bench), thereby bypassing the Chief Justice's administrative role as 'master of the roster'.
respondent_arguments: Judicial discipline and propriety demand that a bench of two judges must follow the decision of a three-judge bench. If they believe a three-judge bench's decision is incorrect, the proper procedure is to refer the matter to another three-judge bench, not directly to a five-judge bench.
The authority to constitute benches is an administrative power vested in the Chief Justice of India, as supported by Article 145(2) and (3) of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand and Others
cases.principle: The Chief Justice is the 'master of the roster' and has the sole authority to constitute benches and allocate judicial business to judges to ensure the smooth functioning of the court and prevent chaos. No judge can take up a matter on their own unless it is allocated by the Chief Justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Chief Justice of India is the master of the roster and alone has the prerogative to constitute Benches and allocate matters. No Judge or Bench can allocate a matter to themselves or issue a direction to the Chief Justice regarding the composition of a Bench.
obiter: Judicial discipline requires a Bench of two judges that disagrees with a decision of a three-judge Bench to refer the matter to another three-judge Bench, rather than directly to a five-judge Bench.
On the judicial side, the Chief Justice is only the first amongst equals, although the administrative control of the High Court vests in the Chief Justice alone.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The administrative authority to constitute Benches is vested exclusively in the Chief Justice of India. Consequently, no judge or bench can issue any command or order directing the Chief Justice to constitute a particular Bench. Any order passed that is contrary to this principle is legally ineffective and not binding on the Chief Justice.
legal_tests_applied: The principles stated in State of Rajasthan v. Prakash Chand and Others (1988) 1 SCC 1, which hold that the administrative control of the court vests in the Chief Justice alone and that puisne judges cannot "pick and choose" cases or give directions for listing that run counter to the Chief Justice's orders, are squarely applicable to the Supreme Court.

The rule of judicial discipline and propriety, which dictates that if a bench of two judges disagrees with a decision of a three-judge bench, the proper course is to refer the matter to another three-judge bench, not directly to a five-judge bench.
Article 145(2) and (3) of the Constitution, which support the administrative power of the Chief Justice regarding the constitution of benches.
why_appellant_lost: The two-judge bench violated "judicial discipline and propriety" by directly referring a matter to a five-judge bench upon disagreeing with a three-judge bench's decision, when the proper course was to refer it to another three-judge bench.

The order passed by the two-judge bench was an impermissible "command or order directing the Chief Justice of India to constitute a particular Bench," which infringes upon the exclusive administrative authority of the Chief Justice.

The action of the two-judge bench ran counter to the established principles that "puisne Judges cannot 'pick and choose' any case" and "no Judge or Judges can give directions to the Registry for listing any case before him or them which runs counter to the directions given by the Chief Justice."
why_respondent_won: The court accepted the argument that the composition of Benches is an administrative power of the Chief Justice, supported by Article 145(2) and (3) of the Constitution and the principles laid down in Prakash Chand.

The court affirmed the procedural argument that "judicial discipline and propriety demands that a Bench of two learned Judges should follow a decision of a Bench of three learned Judges" or, if in disagreement, refer the matter to another three-judge bench.
The court explicitly stated that the principles from Prakash Chand, which vest administrative control in the Chief Justice, "shall squarely apply to the Supreme Court."
policy_considerations: An institution has to function within certain parameters and that is why there are precedents, rules and conventions.
The necessity of maintaining "judicial discipline and propriety" to ensure the orderly functioning of the judiciary and adherence to hierarchical precedent.
